aspectTitle: CSS-reordered visual layout makes DOM/tab order contradict the meaningful order (no tabindex, no script)
aspectDescription: A page uses NO positive tabindex and NO focus-managing script, so every static 'tabindex misuse' heuristic finds nothing. But CSS (flexbox `order`, grid placement, float, absolute positioning) reorders the visual presentation so that the natural DOM tab order no longer follows the meaning conveyed by the rendered layout. G59's core point applies: 'When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.' Judging a violation requires looking at the RENDERED page, inferring the inte
scenario: Single-page e-commerce checkout (Maple & Thread). A flex column whose 'Place order & pay' submit block is authored first in the DOM but pushed to the visual bottom with order:99. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order: T1 = the submit button (at y=1213, the visual bottom), then Quantity, Shipping, Payment — so Tab reaches the irreversible commit before any field.
mechanism: CSS flexbox `order:99` on a DOM-first submit block makes the commit control the FIRST keyboard tab stop while it renders visually last; the operational sequence (fill fields, then submit) is inverted for keyboard users, so focus order does not preserve operability.

aspectTitle: Focus order interleaves between two semantically distinct sections/groups (the canonical Understanding form failure)
aspectDescription: The Understanding's own failing example: a form has a mailing/marketing-data section (name, address, city, state, postal) and a separate newsletter-checkbox section, but the tab order jumps between sections — name, then a checkbox, then street address, then another checkbox. Every field has a correct visible label, correct programmatic name/role, and is fully keyboard-operable; the interleaving can be produced purely by DOM order with no tabindex for a tool to flag. The failure is visible ONLY to an evaluator who understands which fields 'belong together' semantically (mailing-address fields f
scenario: E-commerce checkout (Northwind Outfitters) with two side-by-side boxed sections — Billing address and Shipping address — each visually holding Full name/Street/Apt/City/Postal in order. The whole form is one CSS grid; the DOM emits the two addresses interleaved line-by-line (billing-name, shipping-name, billing-street, shipping-street, ...), so with no tabindex the keyboard focus zig-zags between the billing and shipping cards on every Tab.
mechanism: Focus order interleaves two semantically distinct address groups: pure DOM source order alternates billing-field then shipping-field for each line, so a keyboard user is pulled from the billing recipient to the shipping recipient before finishing the billing block. The fields are placed into their correct visual cards by CSS grid-template-areas, so visual grouping is intact while the focus sequence crosses the billing/shipping boundary on every Tab, destroying the user's 'I am entering my billing address' mental model.

aspectTitle: Focus not returned (or returned illogically) after a dialog/menu is dismissed (F85, close branch + modal return)
aspectDescription: F85's second failure branch and the Understanding's modal example: after the user dismisses an in-page menu or dialog, focus is dumped on document.body (or scrolls to top), forcing the user to tab from the very start of the page back to where they were. The pass condition is nuanced: focus should return to the trigger control, OR — if the trigger was removed by the action — to a logical neighboring element (F85's tag-delete note). Evaluating this requires understanding what the 'logical' return point is given what the action did: deleting an item should move focus to the next item, not the top
scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard (Metrico) 'Dashboard settings' modal. On open, focus correctly moves into the dialog; on close (via ×, Cancel, Save, or Escape — all routed through one closeDialog()), focus is dropped to document.body instead of returning to the 'Dashboard settings' trigger, so the next Tab restarts at the top-of-page header nav.
mechanism: closeDialog() hides the overlay and explicitly blurs/sets focus to document.body without calling openBtn.focus(); F85 'focus is set to the document' close-branch failure — verified by Puppeteer: after Escape, document.activeElement === body and the next Tab lands on the first header nav link (Overview), forcing the keyboard user to tab from the page top back to the toolbar.
primarySelector: #open-settings (trigger that should regain focus); defect in #settings-dialog closeDialog() handler

aspectTitle: Modal dialog focus is not contained — forward Tab or backward Shift+Tab escapes behind the inert backdrop
aspectDescription: The Understanding modal example and TT 4.F step 3 require that for a modal, keyboard focus navigating BOTH forward and backward remains within the dialog until it closes, with outside content inert. The subtle, human-judgment failure: a 'modal' that looks modal (dim backdrop, centered card) and may even trap forward Tab, but Shift+Tab (backward) escapes to the page behind it, or the last element's forward Tab leaks to page content. Because TT says backward order need not mirror forward but must still preserve operability, evaluating containment requires testing BOTH directions and judging whet
scenario: Northbridge Bank 'Confirm transfer' modal (dim backdrop + centered card). A hand-rolled focus trap wraps only the FORWARD direction; the Shift+Tab branch was never written. Forward Tab is perfectly trapped, but Shift+Tab from the first control (the amount field) falls through to the browser default and lands on the page header's 'Log out' link behind the non-inert backdrop.
mechanism: Asymmetric modal containment: the keydown handler on #modal implements only the `!e.shiftKey && activeElement===last` forward wrap and has no backward branch, and the background (header/main) is never made inert/aria-hidden. So backward Shift+Tab from the first control escapes the open modal onto an operable destructive control ('Log out') behind the backdrop, violating TT 4.F step 3's both-directions containment.

The order preserves meaning (each header introduces the group beneath it) and operability (every link reached exactly once, in logical order); nothing receives focus twice and no dead stop interrupts a coupled sequence.
